clue.text: Puffing like this, what with gravity and the slope before us

indicators.note: the slope is placed in front of the word us, so 'before' orders the charade

parts.note: G is the standard symbol for gravity in physics
a ramp is a slope

explanation.surface: Someone struggling uphill, gasping with gravity and a steep slope ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puffing like a grampus' is an old idiom for breathing heavily: a grampus is a small whale that blows noisily, so the clue defines it by the simile.
explanation.definitionFit: A grampus is a blowing whale, the animal named in the idiom for heavy, wheezing breathing.

clue.text: He boasts a hot-air study

parts.note: empty talk, hot air, is gas
to con is to study or learn by heart

explanation.surface: A braggart is one who studies how to talk hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: People from Gascony were proverbial braggarts, so the word came to mean a boaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A gascon is a braggart, from the reputation of the people of Gascony in France.

clue.text: An apple-pie bed on All Fool's Day ? (wrong fruit)

definitions.text: An apple-pie bed on All Fool's Day ? (wrong fruit)

parts.words: An apple-pie bed on All Fool's Day ? (wrong fruit)
parts.note: a prank bed on the first of April is an April cot; the bracket says the fruit named is not apple but another

explanation.walkthrough: An apple-pie bed is a schoolboy prank bed with the sheet folded so the legs cannot get in; on April Fool's Day it would be an 'April cot', which reads as the stone fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is an orange stone fruit, and the word reads as April plus cot, a bed.

clue.text: Old German province produces tail-less dog

indicators.note: the dog's word loses its final letter, its tail

parts.note: a Pomeranian is a small fluffy breed of dog

explanation.surface: An old German region gives its name to a dog that lacks a tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail-less' takes the last letter N off the breed name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomerania was a historic Prussian province on the Baltic coast, now mostly in Poland.

clue.text: Obvious, but not to the Invisible Man

definitions.text: Obvious, but not to the Invisible Man

parts.words: Obvious, but not to the Invisible Man
parts.note: the word for obvious also reads as 'self visible', which the man in H. G. Wells's story is not

explanation.walkthrough: The Invisible Man of H. G. Wells's novel cannot be seen, so his self is not evident.
explanation.definitionFit: Something clear without proof is evident in itself, and literally the invisible man's own self is not visible.

clue.text: Stripped and ran about the community

indicators.note: the word for ran is placed about, or around, the community's letters

parts.note: ran away means fled
EEC is the European Economic Community, often called simply the Community

explanation.surface: A thief strips a village bare and then bolts round the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts FLED around EEC, giving FL-EEC-ED.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to rob or strip them of money, as a sheep is shorn of wool.

clue.text: The craze for loud publicity

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical direction for loud
an ad, advertisement, is publicity

explanation.surface: A loud advertising campaign launches the latest craze.
explanation.definitionFit: A fad is a short-lived craze or fashion.

clue.text: Lifting device for bars

parts.note: the bars are pubs, and the lifting is of a glass to the mouth by bending the arm

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting device' suggests a crane or jack, but it is the arm joint bent in drinking; 'bending the elbow' is slang for drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising a glass in a pub uses the joint of the arm, so 'bending the elbow' means drinking.

clue.text: Strive for one's favourite income ?

indicators.note: the word income is split as 'in come', placing the favourite inside come

parts.note: a pet is a favourite

explanation.surface: Struggling to earn the income one would most like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'income' is read as two words, 'in come', so PET goes inside COME.
explanation.definitionFit: To compete is to strive against rivals for a prize.

clue.text: Red spies scatter in all directions

indicators.note: the letters of red spies are sent every which way, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Communist agents flee in every direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in all directions' rearranges the eight letters of REDSPIES.
explanation.definitionFit: To disperse is to scatter or break up and go different ways.

clue.text: Cooked on special lines

definitions.meaning: eggs can be prepared by stirring them in a pan
a telephone line fitted with a device that garbles speech for secrecy

explanation.surface: A dish prepared to a particular recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the egg dish; the second is a secure phone call, garbled so eavesdroppers cannot follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggs stirred while cooking are said to be scrambled, and a secure telephone line with garbled signals is also described the same way.

clue.text: Overtakes craftily

parts.note: read 'craftily' as 'by craft', boats: in college rowing races a boat overtakes the one ahead by striking it

explanation.walkthrough: In Oxford and Cambridge college boat races (the 'Bumps') a crew passes the one ahead by colliding with it, so the overtaking is done by craft, meaning boats.
explanation.definitionFit: In bumping races a crew that catches and touches the boat ahead is said to have bumped it, the way of overtaking.

clue.text: It's Cora's turn for the trophy

indicators.note: it is Cora's turn, read as her letters being turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Cora is next in line to collect the prize.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of the possessive is a letter here: CORAS rearranged gives the film award.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette given to film-makers is a famous trophy.

clue.text: The Spanish three-quarters in this (or rather some other) place

parts.note: el is the Spanish for 'the'
three of the four quarters of the compass: South, East, West
read with 'place', 'in this place' means here

explanation.surface: A Spanish rugby side's three-quarter backs are somewhere in the vicinity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three-quarters' looks like rugby backs, but means three compass points, S, E and W. The bracket corrects 'in this place' to 'some other place', the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhere else, not at the place in question, is the meaning of the adverb.

clue.text: Put a name to it in the event of my inability, it's important

parts.note: to sign is to put one's name to a document
if means in the event of
I can't expresses the speaker's inability

explanation.surface: Someone asks a deputy to sign on their behalf if they cannot, as it matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something significant is of note or importance.

clue.text: Rules of conduct unsuitable for the Court of Session?

definitions.meaning: the permanent rules governing how a parliament or body conducts its business

definitions.text: unsuitable for the Court of Session
definitions.meaning: instructions to stand up do not suit a court that is in session, or sitting

explanation.walkthrough: The Court of Session is Scotland's supreme civil court; a court in session is sitting, so orders to stand would not suit it.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing orders are the fixed procedural rules of a legislature, and read literally are commands to get up, out of place in a sitting court.

clue.text: Not bespoken, Peggy?

definitions.meaning: not made to order, off the peg
Peggy as a name for a willing housemaid, a ready maid

explanation.surface: A suit not made to measure, for someone named Peggy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bespoken' is bespoke, made to order. Peggy, a typical maid's name, is a 'ready maid', and off-the-peg clothes fit too.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing bought off the rack rather than tailored is ready-made, and the phrase also sounds like a willing servant girl.

clue.text: No doubt they took the cable " Headgear not Livingstone's "

definitions.text: No doubt they took the cable " Headgear not Livingstone's "

parts.words: No doubt they took the cable " Headgear not Livingstone's "
parts.note: ship's winches haul the anchor cable; the quote reads as caps belonging to Stan, Stanley, rather than to Livingstone

explanation.walkthrough: Henry Morton Stanley found the explorer David Livingstone in Africa; headgear that is Stan's, not Livingstone's, is 'caps Stan's'. 'took the cable' suggests receiving a telegram, but the machines wind ships' cables.
explanation.definitionFit: Capstans are revolving drums on ships used to wind in heavy cables and anchor chains.

clue.text: How my, but not your, letters are arranged

definitions.text: How my, but not your, letters are arranged

parts.words: How my, but not your, letters are arranged
parts.note: the letters M then Y run in dictionary order, while Y, O, U, R do not

explanation.walkthrough: 'letters' looks like correspondence, but means the letters of the words 'my' and 'your'.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters set out in the order of the ABC are arranged this way, as M comes before Y.

clue.text: A brown-coated colonel, or so we hear

definitions.text: A brown-coated colonel, or so we hear

parts.words: A brown-coated colonel, or so we hear
parts.note: colonel is said the same as kernel, a nut, and here it is coated in brown caramelised sugar

explanation.walkthrough: 'colonel' suggests an army officer in a brown coat, but the spoken word is kernel: a nut coated in browned sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Praline is a confection of nuts coated in caramelised sugar.

clue.text: Sugar sounds appropriate for Pobbles

indicators.note: the description of the Pobble is said out loud to give the letters entered

parts.note: Edward Lear's poem is about the Pobble who has no toes, so a Pobble would lack toes

explanation.surface: Sugar is said to suit some curious creatures called Pobbles.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's nonsense poem 'The Pobble Who Has No Toes' tells of a creature without toes; 'lack toes' spoken gives the milk sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Lactose is the sugar found in milk.

clue.text: Master awkward current

indicators.note: an awkward version of the word master has its letters in a clumsy, new order

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster finds the present situation difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges MASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A stream is a flow or current of water.

clue.text: One winds up with this on one's plate

definitions.text: One winds up with this on one's plate

parts.words: One winds up with this on one's plate
parts.note: 'winds up' read literally: an Italian pasta that diners twirl round a fork

explanation.walkthrough: 'winds up with' suggests ending up with something, but the diner literally winds the long strands round a fork.
explanation.definitionFit: Long thin pasta strands are eaten by twirling them round a fork, so a diner literally winds them up.

clue.text: Spirits don't have heads on, say the innkeepers

indicators.note: the spirits lose their head, the first letter of the word

parts.note: ghosts are spirits

explanation.surface: Ghosts go headless, according to the landlords.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don't have heads on' removes the first letter G.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosts are those who receive and entertain guests, as innkeepers do.

clue.text: Your return includes a bill for a boat

indicators.note: the turned-round word holds the bill inside it
the word for your comes back, read from right to left

parts.note: thy is the old form of your
AC is an abbreviation for account, a bill

explanation.surface: Your tax return lists a bill for buying a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns THY into YHT, which 'includes' AC to give Y-AC-HT.
explanation.definitionFit: A yacht is a sailing or pleasure vessel.

clue.text: A sign of high-class butter ?

parts.note: a butter here is a creature that butts, a ram, and the ram's sign of the zodiac is the first, top-class one

explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is not the dairy spread but something that butts: the ram, whose zodiac sign opens the list.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ram is the first sign of the zodiac, and rams butt with their heads.

clue.text: Soft ! Henry has a line on a bird

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for soft
Hal is a familiar form of Henry, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal
a rope is a line, especially on a ship

explanation.surface: A hushed call for quiet as Henry puts a lead on a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' means after: A and ROPE follow P and HAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A phalarope is a small wading bird of the sandpiper family.

clue.text: A pick-up, as luck would have it

definitions.text: A pick-up, as luck would have it

parts.words: A pick-up, as luck would have it
parts.note: the rhyme 'see a ... and pick it up, all the day you'll have good luck'

explanation.walkthrough: The old rhyme says to pick up a dropped pin for luck, so the luck-bringing pick-up is a small sharp fastener.
explanation.definitionFit: A pin is the small object the proverb says you should pick up to have good luck.

clue.text: Unusual tests on headgear

indicators.note: unusual tests are tests in a strange form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Odd tests are being run on hats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges TESTS into STETS, then ON follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide-brimmed cowboy hat is the classic example of this headgear.

clue.text: Structure of Ray's flashy neckwear ?

parts.note: a ray is a beam, so a dazzling necktie belonging to Ray could be called a beaming tie, while the whole names a building timber

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' looks like a man's name, but it is a beam of light; the 'Structure' is a roof timber joining the feet of rafters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-beam is the horizontal timber linking the lower ends of a roof's rafters, part of the building's framework.
